courses.kinesthetic_hook: Ten Library Lab help-desk cards: find the file → read the drive label → judge a password → read a link → build a budget sheet → measure typing → fit an attachment → plan backups → check screen contrast → write a safety plan.
courses.lesson_excerpt: Help card DCO-3101: Ana saved a summer photo and the file dialog now says 'not found'. Every file has an address called a path, written from the top of the drive down through folders, like /home/ana/Documents/photos/summer.jpg. That full form is an absolute path because it starts
courses.worked_example: cwd /home/ana/Documents/letters + ../photos/2026/../summer.jpg → /home/ana/Documents/photos/summer.jpg
courses.assignment: Submit lab_dco_paths JSON for DCO-3101: two tasks with cwd, relative path, and resolved absolute path.

syllabus.hook: DIGITAL_CONFIDENCE COURSE_DIGITAL_RC: first-computer confidence for adult and teen learners at a library lab — paths and folders, storage units, password strength, link reading, spreadsheet formulas, keyboard fluency, attachments, 3-2-1 backups, and readable screens. Practice data only. Distinct from GENERAL_IT, which trains support specialists. Not student/teacher E6.

weeks.title: Folders and paths — knowing where a file really lives
weeks.body_md: Help card DCO-3101: Ana saved a summer photo and the file dialog now says 'not found'. Every file has an address called a path, written from the top of the drive down through folders, like /home/ana/Documents/photos/summer.jpg. That full form is an absolute path because it starts at the root, the single slash. Programs also accept relative paths that start from wherever you are standing, called the current working directory. Two dots mean the folder above, and a single dot means here. Standing in /home/ana/Documents/letters, the relative path ../photos/2026/../summer.jpg climbs out of letters into Documents, steps into photos and into 2026, then climbs back out of 2026, landing on /home/ana/Documents/photos/summer.jpg. Walk it with your finger on a drawn tree before trusting it. Windows writes C:\Users\Ana\Documents with backslashes and a drive letter, but the idea of climbing and descending is the same. When a file goes missing, ask two questions out loud: where am I standing, and which way does the path walk from here.
weeks.worked_example: cwd /home/ana/Documents/letters + ../photos/2026/../summer.jpg → /home/ana/Documents/photos/summer.jpg

weeks.title: Storage units — why a 500 GB drive shows 465 GiB
weeks.body_md: DCO-3202 is a NO_AI week; work the division on paper. A patron bought a '500 GB' drive and thinks the store cheated her because the computer shows about 465 GB. Nobody cheated. Drive makers count in powers of ten, so a gigabyte is 1,000,000,000 bytes. Many operating systems count in powers of two, where a gibibyte, GiB, is 1,073,741,824 bytes, and then label the result GB anyway. Divide 500,000,000,000 by 1,073,741,824 and you get about 465.66, the same drive described in a bigger unit. The same confusion bites when deciding whether something will fit. Her phone holds 1,200 photos at about 4.2 MB each, where MB means a million bytes, so the folder is 5.04 billion bytes. In the binary unit that is about 4.69 GiB, and the laptop says 4.5 GiB free. It will not fit, even though '5 GB into 4.5' felt close. Write the unit beside every number, convert both sides to the same unit before comparing, and leave room to spare, because a completely full disk makes most computers slow and unstable.
weeks.worked_example: 500 GB = 500×10^9 B = 465.66 GiB; 1,200 photos × 4.2 MB = 5.04×10^9 B = 4.694 GiB > 4.5 GiB free → does not fit

weeks.title: Passwords and passphrases — strength is length times choice
weeks.body_md: DCO-3303 starts with a sticky note that says P@ssw0rd! and a question: is this strong? Strength depends on how the password was chosen, not on how it looks. If every character is picked at random from a pool, the number of possibilities is the pool size raised to the length, and we measure it in bits: length times log2 of the pool. Four words drawn at random from a 7,776-word dice list give about 51.7 bits. Eight characters drawn at random from the 95 printable keyboard symbols give about 52.6 bits. Twelve random lowercase letters give about 56.4 bits, stronger than either, because length grows strength faster than adding symbols. P@ssw0rd! scores far lower than its nine characters suggest, because guessing tools try dictionary words with common swaps first. The NIST digital identity guidance, SP 800-63B, favours long memorable secrets, checking them against lists of known-breached passwords, and changing them when there is evidence of compromise rather than on a fixed calendar. Use a different secret on every site, and let a password manager remember them.
weeks.worked_example: 4 diceware words: 4×log2(7776) = 51.70 bits; 8 random printable: 8×log2(95) = 52.56; 12 random lowercase: 12×log2(26) = 56.41

weeks.title: Reading a link — the real address is at the right end
weeks.body_md: DCO-3404 is a text message that says a bank account is locked and offers a link. Before tapping, read the address the way a computer does. Skip the https:// and stop at the first single slash after it; what sits between is the hostname. Read the hostname from the right end, label by label, because the rightmost labels say who owns it. In https://account.harborbank.example.verify-login.example.net/session the hostname is account.harborbank.example.verify-login.example.net, and its last two labels are example.net. The bank's name near the left is just decoration chosen by whoever owns example.net, which is not the bank. So the call is: do not open. Real organisations rarely ask you to log in from a message; type the bank's address yourself or use its app. Some country endings use three labels, such as .co.uk, so the rule 'last two labels' is a starting point, and the course's examples use the reserved .example endings so nobody is sent anywhere real. When unsure, show the message to the library desk rather than replying.
weeks.worked_example: https://account.harborbank.example.verify-login.example.net/session → hostname ends in example.net → not harborbank.example → do not open

weeks.title: Spreadsheet formulas — let the sheet do the arithmetic
weeks.body_md: DCO-3505 is a monthly budget written on the back of an envelope that never adds up the same way twice. Move it into a spreadsheet: labels in column A, amounts in column B, one row per item. Rent is 650, food 240, the bus pass 55, the phone 35, and savings 120. Instead of typing the total, write =SUM(B2:B6) and the sheet answers 1,100, then keeps answering correctly when the phone bill changes. =AVERAGE(B2:B6) gives 220, the typical line, and =MAX(B2:B6) finds the largest amount, which belongs to rent. To see how much of the month food takes, divide its cell by the total cell, =B3/B7, and format the result as a percentage: about 21.82 percent. The habit worth keeping is that numbers you typed live in one place and every other number is a formula pointing at them. A total typed by hand goes stale the first time anything changes, and that is how budgets quietly stop matching reality. Save the file somewhere you will find it, with a name that says what and when.
weeks.worked_example: rent 650, food 240, bus pass 55, phone 35, savings 120 → =SUM 1100, =AVERAGE 220, =MAX rent, food share =240/1100 = 21.82%

weeks.title: Keyboard fluency — gross speed, net speed, accuracy
weeks.body_md: DCO-3606 is a NO_AI week because it measures your own hands. Job applications and online forms reward people who can type steadily, so the library runs a five-minute practice passage. Typing speed is counted in words per minute, where a 'word' is defined as five characters, spaces included, so long and short words count fairly. Typing 1,250 characters in five minutes is 250 'words' over five minutes, a gross speed of 50 WPM. Mistakes left uncorrected are subtracted per minute: fifteen errors over five minutes costs three, so net speed is 47 WPM. Accuracy compares correct characters with all characters, 1,235 out of 1,250, or 98.8 percent. Most learners improve fastest by slowing down until accuracy stays near ninety-eight percent, then letting speed return, because unlearning a mistyped pattern takes longer than learning it right. Sit square to the keyboard, keep wrists level, and rest the index fingers on the small bumps on F and J. Record the three numbers each week rather than chasing a single best run.
weeks.worked_example: 1,250 characters in 5 minutes with 15 uncorrected errors → gross 50 WPM, net 47 WPM, accuracy 98.8%

weeks.title: Attachments — why a 19 MB file will not fit under 25 MB
weeks.body_md: DCO-3707: a patron's resume portfolio is 19 MB, the mail service says attachments up to 25 MB, and sending still fails. Email was designed to carry text, so attachments are converted into text with an encoding called base64 before they travel. Base64 turns every three bytes into four characters, so the encoded file is about a third larger: four times the byte count divided by three, rounded up to a whole group. Nineteen million bytes become 25,333,336 bytes, just over the 25,000,000-byte limit, which is why the message bounces even though the file looked small enough. An 18 MB file would encode to 24,000,000 bytes and squeak through. When something will not fit, do not split it into a dozen emails or squeeze the quality until the pictures blur. Upload it to a storage service, share a link with view-only permission, and mention in the message what the link is and how long it will stay up. Never attach other people's personal documents to practice messages; the lab uses only made-up byte counts.

weeks.title: Backups — three copies, two kinds of storage, one away from home
weeks.body_md: DCO-3808 begins with tears: a laptop died and took two years of family photos with it. A simple rule, called 3-2-1, prevents most of these stories. Keep three copies of anything you would miss, the original plus two backups. Store them on at least two different kinds of storage, so one failure type, such as a batch of bad drives, cannot take everything. Keep one copy somewhere else, away from the house, so a fire, flood, or theft leaves something behind. The library's example plan has the photos on the laptop's SSD, a copy on a USB hard drive at home, and a copy in a cloud folder; that is three copies, three kinds of storage, and one offsite. There is a fourth rule people forget: a backup you have never restored is a hope, not a plan. Once a month, pick a random file and open it from each backup. Two copies on the same USB stick are one copy with extra steps, and a sync folder that mirrors deletions instantly is convenient but is not a backup on its own.
weeks.worked_example: laptop SSD + home USB HDD + cloud folder (offsite) → 3 copies, 3 media, 1 offsite; restore tested → plan_ok

weeks.title: Readable screens — measuring colour contrast
weeks.body_md: DCO-3909: the library's new event flyer uses pale grey text, and a patron with low vision cannot read it. Readability can be measured. The W3C's Web Content Accessibility Guidelines, WCAG 2.2, define a contrast ratio between text and background colours. Each colour's red, green, and blue values are converted to a relative luminance, a weighted brightness in which green counts most and blue least, and the ratio is the lighter luminance plus 0.05 divided by the darker luminance plus 0.05. Black on white is 21 to 1; identical colours are 1 to 1. Normal-size text needs at least 4.5 to 1 for level AA, and large text needs 3 to 1. The grey #767676 on white measures about 4.54 and just passes. One step lighter, #777777, measures about 4.48 and fails for normal text, even though most eyes cannot tell the two apart, which is exactly why you measure rather than guess. Use a contrast checker before printing or posting, and remember contrast is one accessibility check among many, not the whole job.
weeks.worked_example: #767676 on #ffffff → 4.54:1 passes AA normal text; #777777 on #ffffff → 4.48:1 fails AA normal, passes AA large

weeks.title: Personal digital safety plan — the page you keep
weeks.body_md: DCO-3A10 asks each learner to leave the Library Lab with one page they will actually use. It names a password manager, because unique secrets for every site are impossible to remember otherwise. It turns on multi-factor sign-in for the email account first, since email is where every other password reset arrives, so whoever controls it controls the rest. It lists the backup copies by media and location, passes the 3-2-1 rule, and records the date of the last test restore. It names a real person or desk to show strange messages to, such as the library's IT desk, so nobody has to judge a convincing scam alone at midnight. It records which colours and font sizes work for the reader's eyes. It never contains an actual password, PIN, or recovery code; those belong in the manager or on paper locked away, not on a page that might be photographed. Mentors check the plan against six or more passed labs and ask the learner to show one step live, such as opening a file from the cloud backup.
weeks.worked_example: password manager yes; MFA on email yes; laptop/USB/cloud backups with tested restore; report phishing to the library IT desk; no real passwords in the plan

courses.kinesthetic_hook: Ten Refurb Bench work orders on donated PCs: size the PSU → populate memory channels → plan RAID → choose MBR or GPT → isolate a fault → match display and cable → size a UPS → image a lab → sanitize drives → file the service report.

courses.worked_example: CPU 125 + GPU 200 + board 50 + RAM 10 + SSD 8 + fans 12 = 405 W × 1.25 = 506.25 W → 550 W unit
courses.assignment: Submit lab_ish_psu_budget JSON for ISH-4101: components, total_w, required_w, chosen_psu_w.

syllabus.hook: IT_SUPPORT_HARDWARE COURSE_DIGITAL_RC: bench-technician arithmetic and decision tables for refurbishing donated computers — power budgets, memory channels, RAID, partition schemes, fault isolation, display bandwidth, UPS runtime, imaging throughput, and media sanitization. Distinct from GENERAL_IT (tickets and operating systems) and HARDWARE_ENGINEERING (circuits and embedded design). Not student/teacher E6.

weeks.title: Power supply budget — parts, headroom, and the smallest adequate unit
weeks.body_md: Work order ISH-4101: a donated tower is getting a graphics card so a youth club can edit video, and the old 450 W power supply is suspect. Start with a parts list and each part's rated draw from its spec sheet, not from a forum guess. The processor is rated 125 W, the card 200 W, the motherboard about 50, two memory sticks about 10 together, the SSD about 8, and the fans about 12, for 405 W. A supply running near its limit gets hot, loud, and less efficient, and real loads spike above their averages, so the bench adds a quarter on top: 405 × 1.25 is 506.25 W. The smallest catalogue unit that covers it is 550 W, so the 450 W supply goes in the parts bin. Bigger is not automatically better, since a 1,000 W unit idling at 60 W wastes money and often efficiency. Check that the new supply has the right connectors for the card, and never open a supply's case; the capacitors inside can hold a dangerous charge long after it is unplugged.
weeks.worked_example: CPU 125 + GPU 200 + board 50 + RAM 10 + SSD 8 + fans 12 = 405 W × 1.25 = 506.25 W → 550 W unit

weeks.title: Memory channels — the slots you choose set the bandwidth
weeks.body_md: ISH-4202 is a slow machine that has two good memory sticks in it. Desktop boards usually have two memory channels, labelled A and B, each a separate 64-bit path to the processor. Each transfer moves eight bytes per channel, so peak bandwidth in gigabytes per second is the transfer rate in megatransfers per second times eight times the number of channels, divided by a thousand. DDR4-3200 in one channel gives 25.6 GB/s; spread across both channels it gives 51.2. The previous volunteer pushed both sticks into A1 and A2, which sit on the same channel, so the machine runs single-channel and integrated graphics, which borrow system memory, crawl. Moving one stick to B2 doubles the path without buying anything. The board manual names the preferred slots, often A2 and B2 for two sticks, and the firmware setup screen confirms the mode after a reboot. Handle sticks by the edges, match the notch to the key in the slot, and press until both latches click; a half-seated stick is a classic cause of beeps and no display.
weeks.worked_example: DDR4-3200 in A2 + B2 → 2 channels → 3200 × 8 × 2 / 1000 = 51.2 GB/s; in A1 + A2 → 1 channel → 25.6 GB/s

weeks.title: RAID — usable space, tolerated failures, and why it is not a backup
weeks.body_md: ISH-4303 is a NO_AI week; build the table by hand. A community centre wants its donated four-bay storage box set up for shared files, with four 4 TB disks. RAID combines disks into one volume with different trade-offs. RAID 0 stripes data across all four for 16 TB and speed, but any single failure loses everything. RAID 1 mirrors the same data on every disk: only 4 TB usable, yet three disks can die. RAID 5 spreads one disk's worth of parity, leaving 12 TB and surviving one failure. RAID 6 uses two disks' worth of parity for 8 TB and survives any two. RAID 10 mirrors pairs and stripes across them, also 8 TB; it is guaranteed to survive one failure and survives a second only if it hits the other pair, so the honest table says one. With large disks, rebuilding after a failure takes many hours and stresses the survivors, which is why RAID 6 suits this box better than RAID 5. Most important: RAID protects against a disk dying, not against deletion, ransomware, or fire, because those damage every copy at once. The centre still needs the 3-2-1 backup plan.
weeks.worked_example: four 4 TB disks: RAID 0 16 TB/0, RAID 1 4 TB/3, RAID 5 12 TB/1, RAID 6 8 TB/2, RAID 10 8 TB/1 guaranteed

weeks.title: MBR or GPT — the two-terabyte ceiling and UEFI boot
weeks.body_md: ISH-4404 is a new 4 TB data disk that shows only about 2 TB of usable space after the last technician set it up. A disk's partition table records where each partition starts and ends. The older Master Boot Record format stores those positions as 32-bit sector numbers, so it can address at most 2^32 sectors. With the common 512-byte sectors that is 2,199,023,255,552 bytes, two tebibytes, and anything beyond is simply unreachable. The GUID Partition Table uses 64-bit addresses, supports far larger disks, keeps a backup copy of the table at the end of the disk, and allows many more partitions. A 4,000,000,000,000-byte disk is larger than the MBR ceiling, so it must be GPT. Disks with 4,096-byte native sectors stretch MBR to 16 TiB, but they are not what the bench usually sees. To boot an operating system from a GPT disk, the PC's firmware needs to run in UEFI mode rather than legacy BIOS mode, a setting in the firmware setup screen. Converting the scheme erases the table, so copy the data off and confirm the backup before you touch it.
weeks.worked_example: MBR limit = 2^32 × 512 B = 2,199,023,255,552 B (2 TiB); 4 TB disk > limit → GPT, boot with UEFI; 4096-byte sectors raise the MBR limit to 16 TiB

weeks.title: Fault isolation — symptom first, subsystem second, parts last
weeks.body_md: ISH-4505 is five machines on the bench at once and a temptation to start swapping motherboards. Good technicians follow the power-on sequence, because each stage that succeeds rules out everything before it. No lights and no fans means the power path: the outlet, the cable, the supply's rear switch, then the supply itself. Fans spinning with beeps and no picture means the board is alive but the self-test failed, most often memory or a processor that is not seated; reseat the sticks one at a time before anything else. A self-test that passes and then complains there is no boot device points at the boot order in the firmware or a disk that is not detected. A machine that boots and then shows a stop error usually blames the last driver or update installed. Random shutdowns only under heavy load suggest heat or an undersized supply, so check temperatures and last week's power budget. Write down the symptom in the customer's words, the stage it fails at, and the cheapest test that would confirm your guess. Replacing parts before isolating the fault costs money and hides the real cause.
weeks.worked_example: T1 fans/no display/beeps → memory_or_cpu_seating; T2 dead → power_path; T3 shuts down under load → thermal_or_psu_capacity; T4 no boot device → boot_order_or_disk; T5 stop error after boot → driver_or_os

weeks.title: Display bandwidth — will the cable carry the mode?
weeks.body_md: ISH-4606: a donated 4K monitor flickers or drops to 30 Hz on a refurbished PC. A screen mode is a stream of pixels, and the cable has a ceiling. Multiply width by height by refresh rate by bits per pixel: 3,840 by 2,160 at 60 Hz with 24-bit colour is about 11.94 gigabits per second. That ignores the blanking intervals between lines and frames, so the true need is somewhat higher, and the honest label is lower bound. Compare it with each link's usable data rate after encoding overhead: HDMI 1.4 carries about 8.16, HDMI 2.0 about 14.4, and DisplayPort 1.4 about 25.92. The 4K 60 Hz mode fits HDMI 2.0 and DisplayPort 1.4 but not HDMI 1.4, which is why the old port falls back to 30 Hz. Double the refresh to 120 Hz and the need becomes about 23.89 Gbit/s, which only DisplayPort 1.4 carries uncompressed here. Cables and ports are both links in the chain: a certified high-speed cable on an old port still runs at the old port's speed, so read both before promising a customer a mode.

weeks.title: UPS runtime — watt-hours, inverter loss, and a graceful shutdown
weeks.body_md: ISH-4707: the community centre's storage box and router should ride out short power cuts and shut down cleanly during long ones. A battery's energy is in watt-hours, and the uninterruptible power supply converts it back to mains power through an inverter that loses some energy as heat. This unit holds two 12 V, 36 Ah batteries, about 864 Wh, and its inverter is about 85 percent efficient. The load measured at the wall is 300 W, so the runtime is 864 × 0.85 ÷ 300 hours, about 2.45 hours or 146.9 minutes. Batteries age, cold rooms reduce capacity, and the last minutes of a discharge are not reliable, so the bench starts a graceful shutdown no later than 80 percent of the computed runtime; here the plan picks 110 minutes. Configure the storage box to listen for the UPS's low-battery signal over USB or the network, and test it by pulling the plug while someone watches. Never plug a laser printer or a space heater into the battery outlets; their surges can overload the inverter.
weeks.worked_example: 864 Wh × 0.85 / 300 W × 60 = 146.9 min; start shutdown by 80% → no later than about 117 min (bench picks 110)

weeks.title: Imaging a lab — unicast one by one versus one multicast stream
weeks.body_md: ISH-4808: forty refurbished laptops need the same 32 GB system image before the library's coding club opens. Image sizes are in bytes and network links in bits, so start by multiplying by eight: 256 gigabits per copy. On a gigabit link that really delivers about 70 percent of its rating, one copy takes about 366 seconds, a little over six minutes. Sending the image to each laptop separately, unicast, repeats that forty times through the same server port: about 244 minutes, more than four hours. Multicast sends one stream that every listening machine receives together, so in the ideal case the whole lab finishes in about the time of a single copy, roughly six minutes. Real networks need switches that handle multicast properly, and one slow or faulty laptop can hold the session back, so plan a fallback to unicast for stragglers. Whatever the method, check one finished machine against a list of expected settings before releasing the rest, and record which image version went onto which serial numbers.
weeks.worked_example: 32 GB image × 8 = 256 Gbit ÷ (1 Gbit/s × 0.7) = 365.7 s per stream; 40 machines unicast ≈ 243.8 min; multicast ≈ 6.1 min

weeks.title: Media sanitization — Clear, Purge, or Destroy before a device leaves
weeks.body_md: ISH-4909 is the second NO_AI week, because a sanitization decision has to be yours. Donated machines arrive full of strangers' lives, and the bench's promise is that nothing leaves with them. NIST Special Publication 800-88 frames the choice with three words. Clear uses ordinary commands to overwrite user-addressable storage, enough when the device stays inside the organisation. Purge uses methods that defeat laboratory recovery, such as the drive's own secure-erase or cryptographic-erase commands, and is the floor when a device leaves your control through donation, sale, or a returned lease. Destroy means the media cannot be reused: shredding, disintegrating, or incinerating, and it is the only answer for a drive that has failed and will not accept commands. Solid-state drives remap blocks behind the scenes, so overwriting the visible space can leave old data in spare areas; rely on the drive's purge commands. Every decision ends with verification and a certificate recording the serial number, method, date, and who did it. A quick format is none of the three.
weeks.worked_example: RB-1001 HDD reuse_internal → Clear; RB-1002 SSD leave_org → Purge; RB-1003 failed SSD → Destroy; RB-1004 HDD leave_org → Purge; each verified with a certificate ID

weeks.title: Refurb service report — fault, fix, sanitization, proof
weeks.body_md: ISH-4A10 closes the term with the document that travels with each refurbished machine. For every device the report gives the serial number, the fault class from the bench's isolation table, and the fix in plain words, such as reseated the memory stick in A2. It records the sanitization method chosen for the drive and that verification passed, pointing at last week's certificate. It notes anything a new owner should know, like a replacement power supply, the memory mode confirmed in firmware, or a monitor that needs the DisplayPort cable for full refresh. The bench also signs one sentence for the whole batch: no customer data was retained, copied, or looked through beyond what the repair required. Technicians who browse a donor's photos to 'test the drive' end their volunteering that day. Mentors review the report against six or more passed labs, pick one machine at random, and ask the technician to explain the fault and the fix while the case is open. A clean report is what lets a school trust a donated computer.
weeks.worked_example: RB-1002: fault memory_or_cpu_seating, fix reseated DIMM in A2, sanitization Purge, verified; customer_data_retained false

syllabus.hook: NETWORKING_INFRA COURSE_DIGITAL_RC: internet-scale infrastructure arithmetic — fiber propagation, IPv6 text and prefix math, bandwidth-delay product, BGP path selection, DNS caching, CDN offload, optical link budgets, availability in series and parallel, and 95th-percentile transit billing. Documentation ASNs and prefixes only. Distinct from COMPUTER_NETWORKING (campus LAN, subnetting, switching). Not student/teacher E6.

weeks.title: Fiber latency budget — light is slower in glass
weeks.body_md: Change request NIF-5101 asks whether a new 1,145 km fiber route between two regional exchanges can promise game servers a one-way delay under six milliseconds. Light in a vacuum covers about 299,792 km each second, but glass slows it by the fiber's group index, about 1.468, so the signal moves at roughly 204,000 km/s. Divide the route length by that speed: 1,145 km takes about 5.6067 milliseconds. That is propagation, and no upgrade fixes it short of a straighter path. Serialization is the time to clock a packet's bits onto the wire: 1,500 bytes is 12,000 bits, which takes 0.012 ms at one gigabit per second and would take ten times longer on a 100-megabit link. Add them for a one-way floor of about 5.619 ms, before any queueing or equipment delay. Route length is not the straight-line distance on a map; cables follow railways and roads, so ask for the measured route. Using the vacuum speed understates delay by about a third and leads to promises the backbone cannot keep.

weeks.title: IPv6 text and prefixes — one canonical way to write an address
weeks.body_md: NIF-5202 began as an outage: two engineers searched the change log for the same router address and missed each other because they had typed it differently. IPv6 addresses are 128 bits, written as eight groups of four hex digits, and RFC 5952 sets one canonical text form so tools and people agree. Write hex in lowercase, drop leading zeros in each group, and replace the longest run of two or more all-zero groups with a double colon, choosing the first run if two are equally long. A single zero group stays as 0. So 2001:0DB8:0000:0000:0001:0000:0000:0001 has two runs of two zero groups; the first one collapses and the result is 2001:db8::1:0:0:1. The 2001:db8::/32 block is reserved for documentation, which is why this course uses it. Prefix math is about counting bits: a site receives a /48, and LAN segments are /64, so 64 minus 48 leaves 16 bits for subnet numbers, which is 65,536 subnets. Never squeeze a LAN smaller than /64; address autoconfiguration expects it.

weeks.title: Bandwidth-delay product — why one connection cannot fill the pipe
weeks.body_md: NIF-5303: a research group pays for a one-gigabit link to a partner 80 milliseconds away and complains that a single file transfer crawls at a few megabits. TCP may only have one window of unacknowledged bytes in flight, then must wait for acknowledgements to return. The bandwidth-delay product says how many bytes the pipe holds: one gigabit per second times 0.08 seconds is 80 million bits, or 10,000,000 bytes. The original TCP header allows a window of at most 65,535 bytes, so the sender stalls after 64 KiB each round trip; throughput is window times eight divided by the round-trip time, about 6.55 Mbit/s here, less than one percent of the link. RFC 7323 window scaling shifts the advertised window left by a negotiated count; a shift of 8 multiplies 65,535 by 256 to about 16.8 MB, enough to cover the 10 MB product. The fix is end-host tuning and checking that no middlebox strips the option, not buying a bigger link.
weeks.worked_example: 1 Gbit/s × 0.080 s / 8 = 10,000,000 B BDP; 65,535-byte window × 8 / 0.080 s = 6.55 Mbit/s; window scale shift 8 (65,535 × 256 ≥ 10 MB)

weeks.title: BGP best path — policy first, then the shorter story
weeks.body_md: NIF-5404 asks why traffic to a partner network leaves through the long transit path instead of the direct one. Border Gateway Protocol routers hear several routes to the same prefix and pick one by walking an ordered list of attributes, stopping at the first that differs. This course uses a simplified order: highest local preference, shortest AS_PATH, lowest origin code with IGP before EGP before incomplete, lowest MED, then lowest router ID. Local preference is the operator's own policy, so it outranks everything about the route's length. Here R1 offers a one-hop path through documentation AS 64500 but carries local preference 100, while R2 and R3 both carry 200, so R1 is out at the first step even though its path is shortest. R2 and R3 each have four AS numbers, a tie, so the origin decides: R2 is IGP and R3 is EGP, and R2 wins. The deciding attribute is origin. Real routers add steps such as weight and eBGP-over-iBGP; RFC 4271 is the reference, and vendor documents list their full order.
weeks.worked_example: R1 lp100 [64500]; R2 lp200 len4 IGP; R3 lp200 len4 EGP → local_pref removes R1, AS_PATH ties, origin IGP<EGP → R2

weeks.title: DNS TTL — planning a change the world sees late
weeks.body_md: NIF-5505 is a cutover: a public website moves to new servers at t = 5,000 seconds and the old servers will be switched off soon after. Resolvers that looked up the name keep the answer for its time to live, and RFC 1034 lets them reuse it without asking again. A resolver that cached the record at t = 3,000 with a TTL of 3,600 seconds will hand out the old address until t = 6,600, so its users see the old site for 1,600 seconds after the change. In the worst case a resolver caches the old answer one second before the change and stays stale for the whole TTL, 3,600 seconds. The fix is planning: lower the TTL to something short, such as 300 seconds, at least one old TTL before the change, so by t = 1,400 at the latest, and raise it again once the new servers are stable. Keep the old servers answering until the worst-case window has passed. A change is not live when the zone file is saved; it is live when the last cache has expired.
weeks.worked_example: TTL 3600; resolver cached at t=3000 → expires 6600; record changed at 5000 → stale window 1600 s; worst case 3600 s; lower TTL by t=1400

weeks.title: CDN offload — the miss ratio is what the origin pays for
weeks.body_md: NIF-5606: a public broadcaster expects 12,000 requests per second for a live results page, each object about 150 kilobytes, and its origin servers sit behind a two-gigabit link. A content delivery network answers from edge caches when it can, and only the misses travel back to the origin. The origin's load scales with the miss ratio, one minus the hit ratio. At a 92 percent hit ratio, 8 percent of 12,000 is 960 requests per second, and 960 times 150,000 bytes times 8 bits is 1.152 gigabits per second, uncomfortably close to the two-gigabit link. Raising the hit ratio to 96 percent halves the misses to 480 requests per second and 0.576 Gbit/s. Four points of hit ratio halved the origin's work, which is why cache keys, longer TTLs for static images, and stripping needless query strings matter. The edge still delivers all 14.4 Gbit/s to viewers, so the CDN contract must cover that. Multiplying by the hit ratio instead of the miss ratio gives a number that looks impressive and is wrong.
weeks.worked_example: 12,000 rps × 150 KB: hit 0.92 → 960 rps, 1.152 Gbit/s at origin; hit 0.96 → 480 rps, 0.576 Gbit/s; edge serves 14.4 Gbit/s total

weeks.title: Optical link budget — loss, margin, and the 3 dB rule
weeks.body_md: NIF-5707 is a NO_AI week: do the decibel arithmetic on paper first. A field team must confirm that optics with a 0 dBm transmitter and a receiver sensitivity of −23 dBm will work over a new 40 km span. Decibels add, which is why engineers like them. The planning coefficients are 0.35 dB per kilometre of fiber, 0.5 dB for each mated connector, and 0.1 dB for each fusion splice. Forty kilometres costs 14 dB, four connectors cost 2, and six splices cost 0.6, for 16.6 dB in total. The light arrives at −16.6 dBm, and the receiver can still read it down to −23, so the margin is 6.4 dB. The backbone rule asks for at least 3 dB of margin to cover ageing, dirty connectors, temperature, and the repair splices a backhoe will eventually require, so this span passes. Counting only fiber loss would claim 9 dB of margin and hide two decibels of connectors. Clean and inspect every connector before measuring, and compare the light meter's reading with the budget.

weeks.title: Availability — redundancy in parallel, single points in series
weeks.body_md: NIF-5808: a regional exchange's design has two core routers sharing traffic, each available 99.9 percent of the time, followed by one power feed at 99.95 percent and one fiber uplink at 99.99 percent. The question from management is how many minutes a year customers should expect to lose. A redundant pair fails only when both members are down at once, so its unavailability is the product of theirs: 0.001 times 0.001 is one in a million, making the pair 0.999999 available, assuming failures are independent. Parts in series all have to work, so their availabilities multiply: 0.999999 times 0.9995 times 0.9999 is about 0.9993991. A year has 525,600 minutes, so expected downtime is about 315.9 minutes, more than five hours, almost all of it from the single power feed. Spending more on routers would barely move the result; a second feed would. Shared causes such as one power strip feeding both routers break the independence assumption and must be designed away.

weeks.title: 95th-percentile billing — the bursts you do not pay for
weeks.body_md: NIF-5909, the second NO_AI week, is a disputed transit invoice. Many internet transit contracts bill on the 95th percentile: the provider records average throughput every five minutes, sorts the month's samples, throws away the top five percent, and bills the highest remaining sample. The course fixture has twenty samples between 289 and 905 Mbit/s. With twenty samples, five percent is one, so the bill uses the sample at sorted index ceil(0.95 × 20) − 1, which is index 18 counting from zero. Sorted, that is 720 Mbit/s, while the 905 Mbit/s burst at the top is discarded. At $0.35 per Mbit/s the charge is $252. Billing the peak would charge $316.75, and billing the mean would undercount the busy hours. A real month has about 8,640 samples, so roughly 432 five-minute periods, about 36 hours, can burst without raising the bill. Know where your provider samples, whether inbound and outbound are compared, and check their arithmetic before paying.
weeks.worked_example: 20 five-minute samples sorted; index ceil(0.95 × 20) − 1 = 18 → 720 Mbit/s × $0.35 = $252; the single 905 Mbit/s burst is free

weeks.title: Backbone design packet — documentation numbers, recomputed
weeks.body_md: NIF-5A10 closes the term with a design packet for the regional backbone that the class has been building. It uses only documentation numbers: an autonomous system number from 64496 to 64511, here 64500, and an IPv6 prefix inside 2001:db8::/32, here 2001:db8:4400::/48. Using a real company's ASN or prefix in a training packet can leak into configurations and hijack someone else's traffic, so the reviewer rejects it on sight. The packet recomputes rather than restates: the 1,145 km route's propagation delay, the availability of the redundant core with its serial power feed and uplink compared with the 0.999 target, and the 6.4 dB optical margin. It cites RFC 4271, 5952, 7323, and 1034 for the behaviour it relies on. The final line says plainly that the packet is a classroom exercise and makes no claim about production peering or real customer service. Mentors pick one number at random and ask the author to derive it at the whiteboard.
weeks.worked_example: ASN 64500, prefix 2001:db8:4400::/48, 1,145 km → 5.6067 ms, availability 0.9993991 vs target 0.999 met, margin 6.4 dB, production_peering_claim false
